props.title: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
props.initialSlug: Born to ride, meant to roam.

sections.content: **Even Cowgirls Get the Blues** (1994) stands as one of director Gus Van Sant's most ambitious yet polarizing adaptations. Following his success with Drugstore Cowboy (1989) and My Own Private Idaho (1991), Van Sant tackled Tom Robbins' supposedly "unfilmable" novel with mixed results. The film's surreal tale of Sissy Hankshaw (Uma Thurman), a hitchhiker with abnormally large thumbs who becomes entangled with a radical feminist ranch, exemplifies the challenges of translating counterculture literature to screen. Like **Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas** (1998), it struggles to capture its source material's psychedelic prose and philosophical tangents.

sections.content: The film's production troubles and critical failure marked a turning point in Van Sant's career. After multiple re-edits and a delayed release, it pushed him toward more accessible fare like **Good Will Hunting** (1997) before returning to experimental cinema with his "Death Trilogy" - **Gerry** (2002), **Elephant** (2003), and **Last Days** (2005). The movie's ambitious visual style, mixing Americana with magical realism, influenced later quirky road movies like Wild (2014) and **American Honey** (2016). SUBHEAD: The Challenge of Counterculture Adaptation

The film represents a specific moment when 1990s independent cinema tried to capture the spirit of 1970s counterculture literature. Like **Where the Buffalo Roam** (1980) and Naked Lunch (1991), it demonstrates how beat generation and hippie-era writing often loses its impact when literally translated to screen. Yet its feminist themes and sexual politics feel oddly prescient, connecting to later works like **Thelma & Louise** (1991) and **Boys Don't Cry** (1999).
